### Conventions I applied to every item (so the owner can re-map)

1. **Nodes are workflow steps**, plus a `start` node (category `trigger`, the caller's `run(...)`) and a `stop` node (category `other`, the StopEvent). Items 7, 8 and 9 are drawn at agent/tool/wrapper level (the engine's own steps `init_run`, `setup_agent`, `run_agent_step`, `parse_agent_output`, `call_tool`, `aggregate_tool_results` are identical for every agent and are described in `ir.notes`, not drawn); item 10 draws one agent's loop at a coarser step level (`build_input` stands for `init_run` plus `setup_agent`, `record_result` for `aggregate_tool_results` plus `handle_tool_call_results`).
2. **`return-type-branch` nodes** (category `condition`) stand for a decision that plain code makes inside a step whose return annotation lists several event types (the step's returned event type picks the successor; LlamaIndex keeps no guard on edges). The model step itself stays category `model`. Where a step's whole job is the check (`validate` in item 2, `handle_schema_approval` in item 6) it is typed `condition` directly. In-step guards and in-step retry loops are drawn as `condition` nodes with type `in-step-guard` / `in-step-retry-loop` (items 2, 6).
3. **Category `human`** = an InputRequiredEvent/HumanResponseEvent pair (item 6). Items 7-10 have no human step.
4. **`features.loops`** = number of distinct back-edge target nodes (loop headers) plus runtime fan-out sites (`ctx.send_event` per item with a collected join: items 4 and 5). Mechanical alternative: count of `loop` edges. `features.branching` = number of `condition` nodes. `features.async` is `[]` everywhere (human pauses are scored through `human` nodes, as in the burr ledger). `features.subworkflows` = nodes of category `subworkflow` (the agent-as-tool and agent-helper wrappers of items 8 and 9, each of which starts a separate agent run).
5. **Effects**: `external` = a call to a third-party search, hosted service, generic tool executor or in-process `exec`; `read` = local index or query-engine read; `write` = persisting a local index; run-scoped context or state writes are `none`; model nodes carry `none` (as in the sibling platforms). Item 1's `handle_tool_calls` is `external` because the tool list is a parameter, although the demo tools are arithmetic.
6. **Routers.** A one-shot "model returns a label or list, code picks the successor" is native (IR `agent` with role `route`/`classify`/`plan` plus `when`, `schemas/workflow.schema.json:L128`), so `llm-router` is not listed (items 3, 4, 9; the same call as the burr and pydantic-graph ledgers). **If the owner's rule is to tag every model-chosen branch, add `llm-router` to items 3, 4 and 9** (item 3 quality gate, item 4 model-named tool per plan item, item 9 plan/answer split). Model-chosen peer transfer with conversation hand-over is `handoff` (item 7); a manager that keeps control and repeatedly delegates is `supervisor-delegation` (items 8, 9).
7. **Line references in `ir.notes`**: a bare `Lx-Ly` always cites the item's primary file (the id's path); every other file is cited by its full repo-relative path with `:Lx-Ly` on each range. **For notebooks the line numbers are lines of the raw `.ipynb` JSON file** (each source line of a cell is one JSON string line, so `sed -n 'N p'` on the file shows it with JSON escaping); the cell text I quote in this ledger is the decoded form.
8. **Caps.** A native verdict presumes an explicit cap where the source has none: items 1, 3, 4, 6 (outer loop) and 9 (outer planner cycle) are limited only by a workflow timeout or by nothing; item 2 has a counter (3); items 7, 8 and 10 inherit the engine's run-wide agent-turn cap of 20 (`llama-index-core/llama_index/core/agent/workflow/base_agent.py:L67`, enforced at `L541-L552`); item 5 states that the per-agent limits are not in the file. Each note says which.
9. **Streaming.** Event and token streaming is a feature of every LlamaIndex workflow run; it is tagged `partial-output-stream` only for item 1, whose notebook has a section whose purpose is streaming the model deltas to the caller (L547-L578). In the other items it is progress logging or demo printing and the note says so.
10. Node summaries are my own words; no prompt text is copied beyond a few words, model and provider names (several vendors) are not copied, and the placeholder key strings that appear in the sources (strings beginning with `sk-` and `llx-`, or a `<Your ... Key>` marker) were not copied. `features.connectors` carries provider or service names only (`openai`, `ollama`, `tavily`, `llamaparse`, `llamaextract`).

### Verdict reasoning in one line each

1. Tool loop with a model-decided number of turns and a streamed reply: needs agent tools and partial output; the 120 s timeout is the only bound.
2. Reducible cycle with a counter cap of three around an extract call and a validating check: lowers to `loop` (maxIterations 3) plus `verify`/`code`.
3. Judge-and-rewrite loop (needs a cap), a fixed three-way parallel fan-out, an all-success join and a selection agent: all in today's node kinds.
4. Plan agent, `map` over the plan items (concurrency 4) with `when`-guarded tool tasks, join, decision agent and a `loop` back to plan (needs a cap).
5. Native decompose-and-combine around a `map`, except that each branch is a ReAct agent with its own tool loop.
6. Task, agent with inner retry, `human` node and an outer rejection loop (needs a cap); pause and resume across processes is the host resuming a suspended run.
7. Each agent is a tool loop; the model's `handoff` tool call moves control and the whole conversation to a named peer; one state dict and one memory are shared.
8. A manager agent delegates by tool call to three agent-wrapped workers and decides when to stop; the wrappers share one state dict.
9. A planner model emits a plan that code executes against worker agents, then control returns to the planner until it stops; workers share one state dict.
10. The model repeatedly writes code that a caller-supplied executor runs at run time; results return to the model; the executor keeps hidden state across turns.

3. **`workflows-py/examples/document_processing.ipynb`: summary and notes changed; verdict unchanged.**
   - A second source quirk was found. `schema` is assigned by `json.loads` before `check_schema` runs (L324-L325), so a reply that is valid JSON but an invalid schema behaves as follows:
     - it enters the except branch with a non-empty `schema`;
     - it sends one more model request, whose reply is unused;
     - it leaves the loop (condition `not schema`, L312) without raising.
   - The consequences:
     - the invalid schema is shown to the person (L351);
     - `state.current_schema` keeps its previous value (it is written only on success, L327-L328);
     - an approval then extracts with that previous value, or fails on the first pass, where it is None (L364-L366).
   - The `validate_schema` summary now says that only JSON decode failures are retried.
   - The verdict `native` stands: an agent with a bounded verify/retry loop, a `human` node at a step boundary (`ProposedSchema` returned at L351, `ApprovedSchema` consumed at L353-L370), and an outer feedback loop that needs an added cap (`timeout=None`, L566). The save/cancel/restore variant (L606-L639) resumes at the latest point, so it is not `checkpoint-rewind`.

Two control edges were added, `research_agent -> stop` and `write_agent -> stop`, because any agent's reply without a tool call ends the run (`multi_agent_workflow.py:L566-L628`), which the extractor's note already said. Features: 21 edges (previously 20); maxFanOut is 4 (previously 3).

### Disagreements and doubts not resolved

1. **The rule for `partial-output-stream`.** I tag it where model token deltas reach the caller during the run, either because the workflow's own code writes them (items 1, 9) or because the example consumes library-emitted deltas live (items 8, 10).
   - Item 7 is untagged: the library emits deltas but the consumer's delta printing is commented out (L306-L308).
   - Step-level progress events (items 4, 6, 7) are untagged as observability, although the brief's wording "tokens/events" could cover them.
   - Item 9 rests on emission alone.
   - Under the openai-agents ledger's rule ("consumed for behaviour"), remove the tag from 1, 8, 9 and 10. Under the smolagents ledger's rule ("streaming option on"), add it to item 7.
2. **`chat-session` on items 1 and 10, and `cross-run-state` on item 10, rest on notebook demo sections** that reuse a caller-held Context. If the owner treats a reused Context as a host convention, remove them; item 10 then returns to the extractor's verdict. Items 8 and 9 build a Context or return the chat history for continuation, but they do not demonstrate a second turn, so they are untagged.
3. **`llm-router` stays untagged on items 3, 4, 7 and 9,** under the extractor's convention, which is shared with the burr, pydantic-graph and langgraph ledgers: a model's typed choice routed by code is native. Other platforms differ:
   - The openai-agents ledger tags `llm-router` on every handoff item. That would add item 7, where the write agent picks ReviewAgent or ResearchAgent (L161) through the handoff tool.
   - The google-adk ledger tags it when a model's free-form output picks among two or more declared agents. That would add items 7 and 9 (the planner picks among three agents, L246-L270, L398-L414).

   The merge should pick one rule across platforms.

6. **Items 3 and 5 probably do not run on the pinned engine** (extractor problem 4, re-confirmed). Their graphs follow the intended flow described in the notebooks.

Under the corpus policy anything under `ee/` would be `redistributable: false` (treated like unknown or ToS). **No selected item is under `ee/`**: `git ls-tree -r --name-only HEAD examples templates docs/src/content/en/docs` lists no `ee/` directory, and a `grep` for `/ee` and "enterprise" over the selected source directories found nothing.

Verdict reasoning that was easy to get wrong:
- Items 1 and 4 keep their human pauses native (node-boundary suspend with a receipt or id payload). The construct is listed only where something else needs it (the sub-workflow call in 1; the sub-agent tool and the catch-all failure hook in 4).

- Item 8 lists `guardrail-tripwire` although a capped loop plus an `assert` approximates it for a one-step agent; the notes say what is missing (lifecycle binding at every model step, a non-error tripwire outcome, feedback into the replayed call).
- Items 1 and 7 list `subworkflow-call` although their children could be inlined at compile time; the notes say so.
- KYC `multimodal-io` is not counted because the default extraction provider is a fixture; the optional OpenAI provider would add it.

## 6. Problems, caveats and unresolved questions

Verbatim problems met during the run:
1. `git ls-tree -r -l HEAD templates | awk '{print $4, $5}' | grep -v 'lock' | head -300` returned: "Command did not complete within its 120s timeout and was moved to the background". With a blob-less clone, `-l` makes git fetch each blob size from the promisor remote. The next command, `pkill -f 'git ls-tree'; ...`, returned "Exit code 144" because the pattern also matched its own shell; afterwards `ps` showed no git process. A first `git ls-tree -r -l HEAD examples/` worked but printed "Auto packing the repository in background for optimum performance." many times (promisor fetches triggering `git gc --auto`). Harmless; the clone now holds 42 packs of 5.7 MiB in total. Names-only `ls-tree` was used from then on.
2. The first `sparse-checkout` (cone mode, root files) put the `.gitattributes` in the tree; the later non-cone `set` removed it, see section 1.
3. The repo checker lists `source.extraction` as `source.extra-key` on all 9 lines and, in canonical mode, rejects the five candidate construct ids (section 5). Expected by the brief; the merge will need to accept both.

Caveats and open questions that bear on the verdicts:
- Item 1: the completeness service that enforces the missing-information round limit and the review service were not read; whether a senior reviewer can escalate again is unverified. The chat agent, API and portal that start and resume runs are host adapters read only at the cited spans.
- Item 2: the ingest workflow and the follow-up route that start a run were read only at the cited spans; the domain schemas, the case store and the Stripe and Intercom adapters were not read. The finalize step was read by its status logic, not line by line.
- Item 3: the specialists' structured-output schemas live in domain files that were not read; the loop has no explicit cap in the file.
- Item 4: the pubsub worker, approval routes and reconciler, the containment registry and the evidence providers were read only at the cited spans or not at all; the workflow consumes an `expired` approval decision (`src/mastra/steps/execute-containment.ts:L37-L57`, declared at `src/schemas/approval.ts:L90`) but what produces it at run time was not found in the files read, and today's `human` node has no deadline, so a converter needs an external resume with that decision or a bounded wait.
- Item 5: whether `iterationCount` in `dountil` counts finished passes (so the cap is four passes) is library behaviour that was not read. Storage is in-memory by default, so a restart loses a paused run.
- Item 6: whether the Mastra workspace skills give the "tool-free" reviewer agent tools at run time was not resolved; if they do, the review step needs `agent-tool-loop` and the verdict changes.
- Item 7: the registration function `addDynamicWorkflow` and the predicate and mapping semantics are library code that was not read; the item reads the JSON as written. The documentation says LLMs and HTTP clients can author such JSON, which is relevant to Foundry's design but untested here.
- Item 8: the defaults of `abort()` when no `retry` option is passed come from the documentation (`retry: true` asks to retry instead of ending), not from library code. All moderation checks are regex or keyword stubs.
- Item 9: documentation-claim verdict; router internals, any iteration cap and the primitives it names were not observed, and the page marks the feature deprecated in favour of supervisor agents.
- All items: hosted model ids in the sources (for example `openai/gpt-5.6-luna`, `openai/gpt-5.5`) are strings in the repository as cloned and were not checked for validity; they do not affect the graphs.

### Decision rules applied (aligned with the sibling verification passes where they agree)

- **`agent-tool-loop`**: any agent whose model emits tool calls whose results feed a later model step counts, as the brief requires strictly. This includes tools an agent inherits from the Mastra instance (workspace tools) and sub-agents exposed as tools.
- **`llm-router`**: a model chooses among **two or more declared agent targets**, whether sub-agents or agents exposed as tools. This follows the google-adk, ag2 and inngest-agentkit passes. The pydantic-graph pass instead folded the router into `supervisor-delegation`; see the open disagreements below.
- **`interrupt-resume`**: the pause happens inside an agent run, for example on a tool call that needs approval. A suspend at a step boundary that resumes with ids or a typed answer is a native `human` node.
- **`chat-session`**: one run per chat turn, with history kept in a memory thread or a case store. **`cross-run-state`**: state that a later, independent invocation reads, such as a file-backed LibSQL memory or case store (the google-adk rule).
- **`guardrail-tripwire`**: claimed only when a validator must act inside a multi-step tool loop, concurrently with the model, or on a live stream. Pre- and post-checks around a tool-free agent with a bounded retry reduce to `code` + `when` + `loop`, which is native. The openai-agents pass treated `output_guardrails.py` the same way.
- **Stubs**: classified by what they stand for, as in the langgraph pass. A fixture provider behind a multimodal model contract counts as a multimodal model step.
- **Real workflow**: the item must model a concrete, runnable configuration from source. A documentation snippet whose primitives are undefined does not qualify.

### Disagreements and doubts not resolved

1. **`llm-router` on a supervisor (item 3).** The verifier followed the google-adk, ag2 and inngest-agentkit rule. Under the pydantic-graph rule, item 3 would carry `supervisor-delegation` only. The construct definitions do not settle this.
2. **Item 6 rests on documentation.** The verdict change depends on documented workspace inheritance and the documented skill tools. The core code that attaches workspace tools to an agent with no workspace of its own is outside the sparse tree and was not read. If inheritance does not apply to such agents, item 6 is native again.
3. **Item 1 is agentic only through stubbed providers.** With the shipped defaults, no model runs: extraction and the risk narrative are fixtures, and the chat agent that starts runs is outside the graph. The item is kept because it meets the loop and human clauses, and because `extract-fields` stands for a multimodal model. A stricter "agentic" bar could drop it or remove `multimodal-io`.
4. **Start triggers left out (items 2 and 4).** Item 2 is started from an inbound webhook through the ingest workflow (`ingest-support-case.ts:L134-L190`). Item 4 is started from a pub/sub worker (`workers/workflow-worker.ts:L148-L150`). Both stay host adapters outside the item, as the extractor decided. A reading that includes the template's own start path would add `webhook-trigger` (item 2) and `event-trigger` (item 4).
5. **Item 4 `agent-tool-loop` is a strict-rule call.** The supervisor's single tool call is forced by its prompt and enforced by hooks. A direct, tool-free call of the investigator would be native but would drop the delegation checks.
6. **Item 8 is the weakest item.** It has one model call, regex and keyword stubs, and a code-critique retry. It meets the loop clause but is the first candidate to drop.
7. **Library semantics not read.** Three behaviours rest on documentation or naming, not on library code:
   - item 5: whether `iterationCount` counts finished passes, which makes the cap 4 or 5 passes;
   - item 8: processor retry and tripwire behaviour, which comes from the documentation;
   - item 7: the `addDynamicWorkflow` semantics.
8. **The deleted item 9 leaves no Mastra network item.** Network routing is deprecated upstream. Only item 3 (a supervisor) represents Mastra multi-agent routing.

### MetaGPT (4)

Why these four. They are structurally different: a static subscription pipeline with capped loops (1), an LLM-routed supervisor over tool-using agents (2), a single agent that plans and runs generated code (3), and a code-driven turn protocol over hidden-role model agents (4). Item 1 is read from the role and action sources rather than from an example script, because the brief names the SOP roles and message pool; at this revision the CLI wiring for it survives only as comments (`software_company.py:L56-L61`) and it needs `use_fixed_sop` on the product manager, which the item notes state. Item 2 anchors on `software_company.py` because it hires the default team. Items 3 and 4 anchor on official example scripts.

Points worth a second reader, all in the item notes with spans:

- Item 1, by static reading: a QA result addressed to the engineer is observed but not acted on (`Engineer._think` has no branch for the RunCode cause), so the loop closes inside QA; any answer except "Engineer", including NoOne for a pass, is re-addressed to QA, so the QA loop's only exit is the round cap of 5; the summarise loop never runs at the default `max_auto_summarize_code = 0`; a bug-labelled requirement is acted on only in incremental mode.
- Item 2: the base `MGXEnv.reply_to_human` is a stub that returns a success string; delivery is left to a host override.
- Item 3: in auto mode a failed task triggers a new planning call and the outer loop has no counter, so a port needs an explicit cap.
- Item 4, by static reading: the environment can tally votes but nothing emits the vote action, and the moderator's parse branches cover only hunt, protect, verify, save and poison, so day votes are stored and acknowledged but never applied; step 18 re-announces the night victims.

### CAMEL (3)

| id (after `camel:`) | pattern | verdict | oracle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `camel/examples/ai_society/role_playing.py#specified-task-user-assistant-dialogue` | task specifier, then AI user and AI assistant alternate until a done marker, a termination flag or 50 turns | `native` | mocked-execution (the example's own run with a STUB model) |

| `camel/examples/workforce/pipeline_workflow_example.py#fork-join-literature-pipeline` | pipeline mode: fixed fork-join (1, 5 parallel, 1) with a coordinator choosing workers and the same quality gate | `via-extension:adaptive-retry+llm-router+dynamic-agent-spawn` | none |

Why these three. The role-playing session is CAMEL's namesake pattern and a clean native bounded loop, with a runnable example-level test. The two Workforce items share one engine but differ structurally: auto-decompose builds its DAG at run time from model output, while pipeline mode takes a code-defined fork-join and keeps only the worker choice and recovery policy model-driven. Both tag `dynamic-agent-spawn` and `adaptive-retry` because all five recovery strategies, including `create_worker`, are enabled by default (`workforce/utils.py:L287-L292`) and are reachable from the quality gate in either mode; the notes say this is a failure-path property and that the example's own sample output shows no failure. Points worth a second reader:

- Workforce scheduling: a code screen turns results containing phrases such as "i cannot" or "not possible" into failures before the quality model sees them (`tasks/task.py:L59-L145`), and quality re-runs stop after `max_retries - 1 = 2` failures, after which the low-scored result is accepted.
- Pipeline mode: the coordinator is also asked for dependency ids; scheduling keeps the builder's edges, but non-empty ids returned by the model replace the `Task.dependencies` that supply upstream results to the worker, so a wrong answer can change what a worker is shown without changing the order.
- Pipeline example: its search task has no search tool, so the five "papers" it forks on are model-written examples.
- The parent result is a plain concatenation of subtask results, although the class doc says the task agent composes results.
- `ChatAgent.max_iteration` defaults to `None`, so tool loops are uncapped; `ChatAgent` also summarises its own history by default once the context passes 50 percent of the limit (noted on the role-playing item as untagged runtime behaviour).

### Conventions applied

These keep this part consistent with the other agentic parts.

- **`llm-router`** is not tagged for a one-shot typed choice that code reads. That covers labels, enum strategies and a validated worker id. Such a choice is an `agent` with an enum output plus `when` guards. Repeated model choice of the next agent is `supervisor-delegation`. The autogen and google-adk parts tag every separate model call that picks the next node. Under their rule, `llm-router` would return on items 1, 2, 6 and 7.
- **`shared-scratchpad`** is tagged only when agents read and write a shared store in a model-decided order (item 2). Fixed-order file hand-over is artifact dataflow (item 1).
- **Failure-path constructs** are counted, as the extractor already did for `dynamic-agent-spawn`. Each such note says which constructs are failure-path only, so a merge that counts only the happy path can drop them:
  - item 6 then keeps `dynamic-dag+agent-tool-loop`, plus `adaptive-retry` once a score falls below 60;
  - item 7 keeps only `adaptive-retry`.

### Disagreements and doubts not resolved

1. **The `llm-router` boundary** (items 1, 2, 6, 7). This needs one corpus-wide rule from the merge owner; see Conventions.
2. **Failure-path constructs** (items 6, 7). If the merge counts only behaviour a default run exercises, then `dynamic-agent-spawn`, `model-generated-code-exec` and `interrupt-resume` leave both items, and `agent-tool-loop` leaves item 7. The extractor's `dynamic-agent-spawn` would fall under the same rule.
3. **The `interrupt-resume` evidence on items 6 and 7.** It rests on `CodeExecutionToolkit` and `SubprocessInterpreter` defaults that were read but not run. In a non-interactive host, `input()` would block or raise `EOFError`. Either way the code is gated by a terminal prompt inside a tool call.
4. **`context-compaction` on item 5, and on every CAMEL `ChatAgent`.** By default the agent summarises its history with a model call once the context passes 50 percent of the limit (`agents/chat_agent.py:L510, L1032-L1066`). The autogen verification reserves the construct for exactly this kind of model summarisation. I kept item 5 `native` because the example does not configure it and a short run never triggers it. A stricter merge would add `context-compaction` to item 5, and possibly to items 6 and 7.
5. **`group-chat` on item 4.** The speaker order is code (the step table), so the item could be lowered natively as nested loops over a per-player filtered transcript. I kept the tag, following the ag2 convention for code-selected group chats.
6. **`features.async` for human steps.** Items 2, 3, 4, 6 and 7 have human nodes and keep `async: []`. Sibling parts split on this: ag2, autogen, langgraph and others add `wait`; crewai, openai-agents, pydantic-graph and others do not.
7. **Static-reading findings that were not run:**
   - the QA dead end (item 1);
   - the unreachable werewolf announcement and the post-game idle loop (item 4);
   - the dropped task after a decompose recommendation in pipeline mode (item 7);
   - the spawned worker's approval prompt (items 6 and 7).
8. **Item 1's scope.** The item models the fixed-SOP role set, which no example or CLI path at this revision wires together. Only the role classes, their comments and the role-level tests exercise it. It was kept because the brief names the SOP roles, but a merge that requires an official runnable entry point would drop it.
9. **Item 7's entry node.** `build_pipeline` (category `transform`) has no inbound edge and no trigger node precedes it. This is consistent with the source, where builder calls start the flow. The checker does not reject it.

Item 6's "oracle" is an auto-mode self-check inside the example that needs live model calls; item 17's is a `node --test` harness check inside the script that also needs live model calls; items 16 and 18 are offline tests with fake sockets or a scripted model (items 16 and 18 covered only for their harness/first test, see item notes).

Judgement calls recorded so the lead can overrule them:

- **handoff vs llm-router**: both are tagged on every handoff item. Handoff is the conversation-ownership transfer; llm-router is the model's run-time choice among declared targets. A one-turn rewrite to a typed enum `agent` plus `when`-guarded successors is native (stated in each item), which is why the multi-turn ownership (items 4, 11, 16) is the part that needs the extension.
- **supervisor-delegation** is tagged only where a manager only delegates and may call workers repeatedly (items 5, 6). Not tagged for the financial writer (it writes itself and only optionally calls analysts, item 10) or the hosted root agent (one delegation round, item 14).
- **agent-tool-loop on hosted tools**: the `search_agent` in items 9 and 10 carries the hosted `WebSearchTool`, so it is not "one narrow typed call without tools". A decomposition into a search `task` plus a summarising `agent` is native but fixes the query, so I called it a redesign.
- **cyclic handoffs** (item 11) are not tagged `unstructured-cycle`; they compile to a bounded dispatch loop over a typed next-agent state, and the model-chosen tool-call target is the construct.
- **unbounded source loops** (items 2, 4, 7, 11, 16): the chat/judge `while True` loops have no code-enforced bound outside auto mode. For the judge loop (item 2) I call it native with an explicit imposed cap (5, from the evaluator prompt); chat loops are tagged `chat-session`.
- **streaming** is claimed (`partial-output-stream`) only where streamed content is consumed for behaviour (items 4, 8, 16, 18). The streamed writer in items 9 and 10 only drives a progress display, so no stream construct is claimed there.
- **model-generated-code-exec**: the shell-capable sandbox agents (items 12, 17) and the programmatic-tool program (item 13). Item 13 is trivially re-expressible natively because its arithmetic and SKU list are fully specified; the item records the source's semantics.

## 4. Patterns absent from these sources

Searched file names across the full git tree of both repositories and text across the checked-out example subsets for group chat / speaker selection, shared-state reducers, checkpoints, rewind, fork and time travel. Result: **none of group-chat, state-reducer, checkpoint-rewind appears in the openai-agents example sets.** The only hits were unrelated (the substring "replay" inside `ensurePlaybackNode` in a browser script, a JS test named for preventing approval replay, a cached-state replay to a new subscriber in a session manager test, and "speaker" meaning audio output). There is also no `examples/voice/` directory at the pinned Python sha. Run-state serialisation in the HITL examples is interrupt-resume, not rewind: it resumes the single latest state and offers no earlier-state fork. Limitation: text search covered only the checked-out subsets, and file-name search covered the full trees; `docs/` prose was not read.

The SDK's core packages (outside `examples/`) were not read, so this is a statement about the examples as workflow sources, not about SDK capability.

## 5. Problems and caveats (verbatim where an error was printed)

1. **Checker rejects the requested `source.extraction` object.** Running the repo checker on the output as delivered: `node research/corpus-20261006/scripts/check-items.mjs /var/tmp/foundry-work/corpus-agentic/openai-agents.jsonl` printed `18 lines, 0 valid, 18 invalid` with `source.extra-key: 18` (`line 1 openai-agents:openai-agents-python/examples/agent_patterns/deterministic.py: unexpected source.extraction`). The same file with `source.extraction` removed passes: `18 lines, 18 valid, 0 invalid`. `SOURCE_KEYS` in `check-items.mjs` (and the merge) need `extraction` added, or the merge must strip it. I followed the task's field list and did not edit the checker.
2. **Canonical mode flags the new construct ids.** `node check-items.mjs <copy without extraction> --canonical` printed `18 lines, 4 valid, 14 invalid (canonical mode)` with `ir.vocabulary: 14` (e.g. `non-canonical construct(s) handoff, llm-router, partial-output-stream`). That is expected until the 15 candidate agentic ids are added to `CONSTRUCTS`. The other canonical rules (feature equality, sorted async, unique ids, redistribution) passed for all 18.
3. **First sparse-checkout attempt failed:** `fatal: 'examples/sandbox/handoffs.py' is not a directory; to treat it as a directory anyway, rerun with --skip-checks`. Cone mode only takes directories; I re-ran with `--no-cone` patterns (command above). Nothing else was affected. The `--no-cone` mode also left the JS checkout with more directories than needed (`sandbox/` in full, `realtime-server-controlled/`, `tools/`), harmless at 960 KB.
4. **Features recomputed vs given:** `nodeCount`, `edgeCount`, `maxFanOut`, `humanSteps`, `effects`, `hasCode`, `hasModelCalls` were computed from each graph with `graphFeatures`; `branching`, `loops` are my counts (never below the graph minimum); `async` is `[]` for all items (no schedule/webhook/poll/event start exists; chat/voice sessions are covered by `chat-session`, not by an `event` async token; a deliberate choice so the merge does not infer an event-trigger).
5. **Evidence limits.** Verdicts are readings of source, not compiled or executed. Where a hosted or provider-side behaviour is involved (hosted web search, provider compaction, hosted multi-agent, Live delegation) the behaviour is taken from the example's code, comments and README, not observed. Tests were read only where stated in each item's oracle notes (item 18: mock harness and first test; item 16: test file header and assertions).
6. **Source inconsistency recorded as observed:** `financial_research_agent/agents/writer_agent.py:L37-L38` has a comment saying analyst agents are attached as handoffs, but `manager.py:L193-L205` attaches them with `as_tool` and the README says tools. Item 10 follows the code.
7. **Model ids and fixture data:** example source names current model ids (for example gpt-5.x and a Live model); none is recorded as an executor choice here. Fixture strings that look like personal data (a synthetic SSN-shaped value in `tax_prep.py` and `basic/tool_guardrails.py`, fictional emails) were not copied. A scan of the output for `ssn|123-45|@x.com|api key|bearer|password|secret` found no hit (one benign "tokens" in a summary about token savings).
8. **Line-span hygiene:** two combined `cat -n` listings numbered files continuously (financial_research_agent README + manager.py, and live/agent.ts + delegation.ts). Those spans were re-derived with `grep -n` / `sed -n` per file, and every span in the output was then range-checked by script (section 6). The range check proves a span lies inside its file, not that it points at the right lines; the key claims were spot-checked by hand against the source.

**Disagreements and doubts not resolved (kept as the extractor had them unless stated):**

1. *Item 2 `native` rests on an imposed cap.* In interactive mode the source loop is `while True` with no code bound (llm_as_a_judge.py:L51, L56). The only bounds are the auto-mode cap of 3 (L75-L79) and a prompt asking for a pass after about 5 attempts (L36). I accept native under the rule "bounded reflection loop is native" with the cap the item states. If the corpus treats an unbounded source loop as non-native, no candidate id fits: `unstructured-cycle` is for multi-entry cycles.
2. *Item 17 `shared-scratchpad` is plausible, not certain.* All three agent runs share one sandbox session and workspace (memory-multi-agent-multiturn.ts:L120, L133, L138, L143), and GTM turn 2 rereads notes written in turn 1 through it. But the README describes "separate workspace memory layouts for two agents sharing one sandbox workspace" (examples/sandbox/README.md:L21), both agents are told to keep their notes apart (L97, L108), and neither agent reads the other's notes. If shared-scratchpad requires reads across agents, this is an FP and the verdict becomes `via-extension:agent-tool-loop+model-generated-code-exec`.
3. *`supervisor-delegation` in items 5 and 6 is borderline.* The managers only delegate and decide when to stop (agents_as_tools.py:L32-L36; agents_as_tools_conditional.py:L60-L65). In practice that is one pass, each worker called once, so the tag adds little beyond agent-tool-loop+agent-as-tool. Kept per the definition.
4. *handoff and llm-router are correlated.* In items 4, 11 and 16 every multi-target handoff carries both tokens. The extractor's notes concede that a one-turn typed classifier plus `when` guards is native, as is classify -> route in COVERAGE §6. llm-router stays because the conversing agent itself picks the target mid-turn through a tool call. A merge may prefer to derive llm-router from multi-target handoff rather than count it separately. The item 12 removal follows the same reading: a single target means no routing. If the lead's convention is that any model-initiated transfer is a router, restore it there (counts would be llm-router 4, FP 0).
5. *agent-tool-loop in items 9 and 10 rests on the hosted `WebSearchTool`* (research_bot/agents/search_agent.py:L16; financial_research_agent/agents/search_agent.py:L24), which the provider runs inside the model call. That still exceeds `agent` = one call without tools, so it is kept. Provider behaviour is taken from the code and not observed.
6. *Item 16 input streaming.* Microphone audio arrives as a continuous chunk stream with server-side VAD (server.py:L124-L135, L511-L515). Only multimodal-io and chat-session cover it. The canonical `stream` construct (continuous message streams) was considered and not added. Barge-in cancellation (L131, L662-L663) is not a construct in the list. It is noted in ir.notes, not claimed.
7. *Triviality bar.* Items 13 (one agent run: a model-authored program fans out nine tool calls, then a second model turn) and 15 (one agent over five scripted prompts with provider compaction) meet the letter of the rule: a tool loop with a model-authored fan-out, and five model calls in a loop. Each is also the only exemplar of its construct shape in this platform. A stricter bar ("several distinct agents") would drop both. Kept, flagged.
8. *Oracles of items 6 and 17* are self-checks inside the example scripts that need live model calls (agents_as_tools_conditional.py:L143-L153; memory-multi-agent-multiturn.ts:L147-L159). They stay labelled `test-profile`, but they are not offline oracles. Item 18 stays `mocked-execution`: live.test.ts drives `DelegationHandler` and the order agent with `ScriptedModel` and fake sockets (L18-L59, L98-L145).
9. *Item 14 semantics are provider-side.* Subagent creation, `max_concurrent_subagents` and the `multi_agent_call` items are read from the example's config and logging code (L45-L48, L53-L69). The experimental hosted model was not run, and its docs were not read.

Platform slug `openai-swarm`. Items: `openai-swarm.jsonl` (7 lines, `foundry-corpus-item/1`, sha256 `32662276f16c9d2937a7f4ae84e7133e3bd32d1ec11fdd63d19551dfeaf31af9`). Retrieved 2026-10-07. The only programs run were this session's throwaway scripts (they read the cloned files as text and write the JSONL) and the repo's own `research/corpus-20261006/scripts/check-items.mjs` (read-only on the JSONL).

## 5. Modelling conventions (read before comparing with other clusters)

- **Node granularity.** One node per agent, one per tool function, a human `user_turn` and an output `reply` for REPL-driven examples. A handoff function is not a node: a handoff is a `control` edge between agents. Back-handoffs and tool-result returns are `loop` edges, so removing `loop` edges leaves a DAG (checked for all 7 items).
- **Effects.** Tools in items 1-5 are stubs that return constant strings or print. `effects` names the operation each tool stands for (refund = write, email = external, lookup = read) and the node summary says "Stub". This differs from a literal reading (every stub would be `none`). Reviewers who want the literal reading should recompute the effect counts.
- **`escalate_to_agent` is not a human step.** The airline policy says to escalate to a human, but the function only returns a string (`examples/airline/configs/tools.py:L1-L2`). It is an `action`, so the only `human` node in the REPL items is the user turn.
- **`features.branching`** counts agents that declare at least one function (a model-decided call-or-answer choice) for items 1-5, and flag or model decisions for items 6-7 (plan vs answer, approval flag, iterate flag, evaluate flag; run status). **`features.loops`** counts source iteration constructs: the REPL `while True` plus the `Swarm.run` loop for items 1-5; the loop nodes for items 6-7. The merge recomputes graph-derived fields anyway.
- **Verdict basis for REPL items.** `run_demo_loop` is `while True` with no exit and the caller carries messages and the active agent between `Swarm.run` calls. Under the owner's bounded-semantics rule (an infinite process becomes triggered runs that carry state) that is `chat-session` + `cross-run-state`. Sensitivity: if a reviewer prefers to treat the REPL as one bounded `loop` over `human` turns in a single run, those two tokens drop from items 1-5, except that `cross-run-state` stays for item 4 because of the SQLite file. The remaining tokens do not change.
- **Handoff is not `subworkflow-call`.** Control is transferred and never returned to a caller; return is another explicit transfer.
- **Unbounded source loops.** `max_turns` defaults to `inf` (`swarm/core.py:L239`), the REPL has no exit and plain plan execution in item 6 is capped only for re-plans. Foundry needs caps on every loop; each item's notes say so.

### Construct use

Counts over the 7 items: agent-tool-loop 7, chat-session 5, cross-run-state 5, handoff 4, llm-router 4, unstructured-cycle 3, dynamic-dag 1, partial-output-stream 1. Existing ids: chat-session, agent-tool-loop, cross-run-state, unstructured-cycle, dynamic-dag. Candidate new agentic ids used (exact spellings): `handoff`, `llm-router`, `partial-output-stream`. No `new-*` id was needed. Order inside a verdict: existing ids in registry order, then new ids in the order of the task list.

Considered and not used, with reason:

| construct | why not |
| --- | --- |
| interrupt-resume | Item 6's approval gate sits between plan steps (`local_engine.py:L177-L191`), so a `human` node placed by expansion covers it. `execute_tools=False` (README `execute_tools` row, `core.py:L275`) interrupts a tool call but no shipped code resumes after it (evals only inspect the call). |
| state-reducer | The framework merges per-call `context_variables` with `dict.update` (`core.py:L133`), but no example function returns a `Result`, so nothing is ever written. `run_demo_loop` also resends the original dict every turn (`repl.py:L76`), so updates would not persist across turns. |
| supervisor-delegation, group-chat, agent-as-tool, dynamic-agent-spawn | Triage transfers the conversation and does not collect results or loop until it decides to stop; speaker choice is a transfer by the current agent; no agent is called as a tool; agents are fixed at import. |
| shared-scratchpad | Agents share the message history, not a board; context variables are read-only in every example. |
| guardrail-tripwire | Policy exists only as prompt text. Item 6's start-up validation checks configuration, not run-time input or output. |
| context-compaction | History grows without trimming in every example. |
| model-generated-code-exec | Item 6 imports a handler whose directory name comes from the plan, but the code is a local file, not model-written. |
| checkpoint-rewind, multimodal-io | Absent from all sources read. |

## 6. Evidence classes and gaps

- **Observed code.** Every node, edge, loop and effect comes from the pinned files; spans are in `source.extraction.spans` and in each `ir.notes` (paths relative to the example directory, `swarm/` and `tests/` for the library, "repo README.md" for the root README). All spans were machine-checked against the line counts of the checkout.
- **Documentation claims.** README statements: Swarm is stateless between calls (repo README.md:L81); only the active agent's instructions are in the system prompt after a handoff (L167); only the last handoff function counts when several are called (L279); `max_turns` is described as "conversational turns" (L133) while the code counts messages (`core.py:L154`, `L257`).
- **Inference.** (a) Item 4: the triage agent comes from `swarm.agents.create_triage_agent(agents=[sales, refunds], add_backlinks=True)`, a module that does not exist at the pinned commit (`git ls-tree` over the whole tree). Triage-to-specialist and specialist-to-triage edges, `handoff`, `llm-router` and `unstructured-cycle` for this item rest on the call site and the example README. (b) Item 4 passes `description=` to `Agent`, which defines no such field (`swarm/types.py:L14-L20`); that pydantic ignores extra keyword arguments was assumed, not run. (c) All IR verdicts are static judgments against the Phase 1 IR (`schemas/workflow.schema.json`, `research/core-20261006/DESIGN.md`), not compile or run results.
- **Unavailable.** `swarm/agents` (the missing helper), repository history before the pinned commit (depth 1), a live OpenAI model, Qdrant, any execution of the eval suites.

## 7. Observed defects and negative results (static reading, nothing executed)

Kept so that later runs do not mistake source defects for Foundry defects.

Item 1, airline
- The `STARTER_PROMPT` in force is the one from `data/routines/prompts.py` (imported last, `configs/agents.py:L1-L4`). It tells the model to call a `change_intent` function that does not exist (`prompts.py:L12`); the working back-link is `transfer_to_triage`.
- `valid_to_change_flight` and `initiate_baggage_search` always report the positive outcome (`configs/tools.py:L5-L7`, `L27-L28`), so the "not eligible" and "not found" policy branches cannot occur through the tools. `escalate_to_agent` does not involve a human.
- Recorded 2024 eval outputs in the repo (`evals/eval_results/`): triage 4 runs of 20/20; flight modification 5/15 (2024-05-15, twice) then 15/15 (2024-05-20). Run 1 uses older sentences and the model asked a clarifying question instead of transferring for both the change and the cancel request. Run 2 contains a fixture error: a cancel request is expected to call `transfer_to_flight_change`, the model correctly called `transfer_to_flight_cancel` and was scored wrong, and the plain change request again got a question instead of a transfer. The 2024-05-20 run, whose cases equal the current `eval_cases/flight_modification_cases.json`, passes 15/15. Negative result kept: routing from a short request depends on prompt and fixture wording. Not re-run here.

Items 2-3
- `triage_agent/agents.py:L36-L41`: `transfer_to_sales` and `transfer_to_refunds` have no docstrings, so the model sees only the names.
- Support bot compose file publishes only port 6335 (`docker-compose.yaml:L6-L7`), while `main.py:L11` connects with the client's default port (not read in this checkout; believed to be 6333). The streaming example's compose publishes 6333 and 6334. Unverified.

Item 4, personal_shopper
- The script cannot start from this commit (`main.py:L6` imports a missing module).
- `refund_item`, `order_item`, `notify_customer` return `None`; the library turns that into the string `"None"` (`core.py:L81-L83`), so the model learns outcomes only from console prints. `refund_item` prints "Refund initiated" even when no purchase was found (`main.py:L27-L29`).

Library (affects items 1-5)
- `handle_tool_calls` does not catch exceptions from a tool or from `json.loads` of the arguments (`core.py:L114`, `L122`): a failing tool aborts the whole run. Foundry's `onError` has no counterpart here.
- In streaming mode the stored message is labelled with the starting agent (`core.py:L158`) while the streamed delta uses the active agent (`L183-L184`).
- `max_turns` counts appended messages, assistant and tool alike, not turns.

Item 6, local engine
- The tool name from the model output becomes a filesystem path and the handler is imported without checking membership in the assistant's tool list; the approval flag defaults to false for unknown names (`local_engine.py:L177`, `L208-L216`). A guardrail gap.
- Judge result handling: when the judge returns a real boolean `True` the success flag stays `False` (`local_engine.py:L274-L275`); the judge reply is coerced with a blind quote replacement (`assistants.py:L62`), so apostrophes in the message break parsing.
- Despite the directory name nothing streams (`utils.py:L7` default `stream=False`; no caller sets it).

Item 7, Assistants API engine
- It reads `assistants/` and `tools/` (`assistants_engine.py:L31-L32`) but the example ships `configs/assistants` and `configs/tools`.
- A new assistant is created only when one with that name already exists (`L66-L75`), so on a fresh account the wrapped instance is `None`.
- Only the first tool call of a `requires_action` batch is answered (`L165`).
- Handlers are called with a `tool_id` argument (`L202`), but `submit_ticket_assistants` takes only `description`, and `query_docs` and `send_email` define no `*_assistants` function.
- The test loader requires a `groundtruth` key (`L353`) that 3 of the 4 shipped test lines lack, and `main.py:L27` routes `--test` to the local engine anyway.
- The poll loop has no timeout or cap (`L154-L172`).

### 10.4 Disagreements and judgement calls not resolved here

1. **`cross-run-state` on the REPL items (1, 2, 3, 5).** Kept. The `run_demo_loop` caller carries the whole message history and the active agent between `Swarm.run` calls (`swarm/repl/repl.py:L86-L87`). Review 02 §3.E2 models each chat turn as one run whose history lives in E1 session state, and the corpus lists conversation memory under `cross-run-state`. The sibling `openai-agents` cluster tags its REPL loops `chat-session` only. The merge should normalise one way. Dropping the token would take this platform's `cross-run-state` count from 4 to 0.
2. **`unstructured-cycle` for back-handoffs (items 1, 2).** Kept: the agent graph is cyclic with several entry points, because the REPL resumes at the last active agent. The sibling `openai-agents` `customer_service` item, which also transfers back to triage, does not tag it. If `handoff` is implemented as a group node with an active-agent pointer and a turn cap, the cycle becomes internal to it and this token drops.
3. **`llm-router` boundary.** I count it only when there are two or more declared targets the model can choose between. Other cluster ledgers count it "for routers re-entered in a cycle or choosing among agents with conversation transfer". Item 3 sits on that boundary.
4. **Item 6 `native`.** This rests on two readings. First, a model-produced list of calls over a closed tool set is data dispatched by a fixed body, not a `plan/expand` fragment. Second, a declared step cap is acceptable where the source relies on the completion token limit. A reviewer who treats any LLM planner as `dynamic-dag` would restore that token. The free-text plan parse (`src/runs/run.py:L20-L41`) would become a typed schema, which is stricter: an unknown tool name is rejected instead of returning "No tool file found".
5. **Effects convention.** Kept as the extractor documented it: a stub tool gets the effect of the operation it stands for, the REPL `user_turn` is `read` and `reply` is `write`. A literal reading would give `none` for the stubs and change the effect counts.
6. **Item 5 kept, borderline.** It has a single agent with two stub tools, and its README calls it a function-calling demo (`examples/weather_agent/README.md:L3`). It meets the "loop or human step" criterion and is the only `partial-output-stream` item. Drop it if the cluster should hold only multi-agent workflows.
7. **Item 7 kept, although it cannot complete a task as shipped:**
   - wrong config paths (`L31-L32`);
   - inverted assistant creation (`L66-L75`);
   - missing `*_assistants` handlers;
   - an unusable test loader.

   Its control flow is fully readable, and the pattern (hosted run, then client-side tool fulfilment by polling) appears nowhere else in the set. If the corpus requires examples that can run at the pin, drop it on the same grounds as item 4.
8. **Oracles.** `test-profile` on items 1, 2, 5 and 6 means shipped evals that need a live, non-deterministic model; none was run. They are not deterministic oracles.
9. **`features.async` of item 7** is `["poll","wait"]` and describes in-run polling, not a trigger. It is kept; the merge must not read it as `poll-trigger`.

```sh
git sparse-checkout set --no-cone /pydantic_graph/ /docs/graph.md /docs/graph/ /docs/multi-agent-applications.md /docs/deferred-tools.md ... (docs, examples)
git sparse-checkout add /examples/LICENSE /src/pydantic_ai_harness/LICENSE /src/pydantic_ai_harness/examples/ /docs/persistence.md /tests/test_examples.py /examples/pydantic_ai_examples/ag_ui/ ...
```

No Git LFS, no submodules, no package install, no install hook, no notebook, no cloned code executed. The only code run
was this task's own throwaway generator and validator in the session scratchpad, which import `parseVerdict`,
`findSecret`, `validateItem` and `graphFeatures` from `research/corpus-20261006/scripts/check-items.mjs` (read-only import).
Nothing in the Foundry repo was edited and no git state of it was touched. The full sparse-checkout list is in
`git sparse-checkout list` inside the clone. The repo tree has 4,175 files; 111 were checked out.

  (`docs/graph/builder/index.md:L325-L328`). The old persistence docs, `FullStatePersistence` examples and the old
  `question_graph` human-in-the-loop example are therefore **not present** at this revision (no `question_graph` path in
  `git ls-tree`; no persistence module under `pydantic_graph/pydantic_graph/`). The shallow clone cannot reach older history.
  Checkpoint and resume now live in the harness `StepPersistence` capability and in durable-execution backends.
- `docs/graph.md` now documents `BaseNode` classes registered on the new `GraphBuilder` (`g.node(...)`, `g.build()`), plus the
  builder API under `docs/graph/builder/`.
- The repo tests run doc fences with mocked models (`tests/test_examples.py`), but skip everything under `docs/harness/`
  (`tests/test_examples.py:L126-L128`) and never collect `examples/`.

Why these: each has at least one of a model loop, router, hand-off, human step or interrupt, and together they cover the
platform's distinct patterns: reflection loop (1), human FSM with an irreducible cycle (2), fork/join with reducers (3),
programmatic hand-off with human decisions (4), supervisor delegation (5), approval interrupt and resume (6),
model-authored orchestration code (7), triggers plus shared store (8), realtime/multimodal hand-off (9), checkpoint and fork (10).

Counts above target: the brief said about 6; I selected 10 because each covers a construct or structure none of the others
does. Items 2 and 3 are weak on "agentic" (no model calls) and are kept because they are the platform's own examples of
the state-machine cycle and of join reducers. Items 7 and 10 are doc-level scenarios assembled from fences, not shipped scripts.

### Verdict reasoning in one line each

1. Reducible single-entry cycle lowers to a bounded `loop` of two `agent` nodes; the source has no iteration cap, so a cap is added.
2. `select_product <-> purchase` can be entered from `coins_inserted` at either node, so it is irreducible; needs the state-machine form of unstructured-cycle.
3. `map` plus `code` folds; native only because reducers are commutative folds after the fan-out and nobody reads shared state mid-run; the reducer-writes-shared-state case that would need `state-reducer` is flagged in the notes, not exercised.
4. The model decides whether and when to call a tool that is itself an agent; the rest (validator retry, human loops, fixed hand-off) is native with caps added.
5. The triage model repeatedly delegates to worker agents and decides when to stop; a one-shot classify-then-route would be native, so `llm-router` is deliberately not listed.
6. The pause happens inside the agent's tool loop after some of the model's tool calls already ran, so a `human` node boundary cannot express it.
7. The call structure is authored by the model at run time as code.
8. Two trigger kinds, a tool-using agent, and a store that outlives runs.
9. Speech in and out, and an event stream consumed while the model runs; the hand-off itself is a fixed sequence passing history as data, so `handoff` is not listed.
10. Snapshots of message history are saved at settled steps and later runs continue or fork from them; the doc itself says these are message checkpoints, not graph-state checkpoints, and that external side effects are not undone.

- All 10 lines parse as JSON; ids unique; node ids unique; every edge endpoint is a node id; no isolated nodes.

## Problems and caveats (verbatim list)

1. `check-items.mjs` does not accept the `source.extraction` object the brief requires: running it on the delivered file prints
   `10 lines, 0 valid, 10 invalid` with `source.extra-key: 10` and `unexpected source.extraction` on every line (`SOURCE_KEYS`
   lacks `extraction`; neither `merge-items.mjs` nor `ITEM-SCHEMA.md` mentions it). I kept the field as instructed. The merge
   step must either allow it or strip it.
2. State persistence and the human-in-the-loop `question_graph` example from the platform brief do not exist at this revision
   (persistence was removed in V2); see "State of the platform" above. Not recovered from history (depth-1 clone).
3. Oracles: only items 1, 2, 3 and 6 map to repo-shipped tests (`tests/test_examples.py` runs the doc fences under mocked models and
   compares printed output); I did not run them. Items 7 and 10 are in `docs/harness/`, which the repo tests exclude; the others have
   no test. For item 1 the critic mock approves at once, so the loop-back edge is not exercised.
4. All verdicts and graphs are my reading of source, not compiled or executed. Item 3 and item 1 `native` verdicts carry stated
   conditions (commutative reducers; an added iteration cap).
5. Item 2 and item 3 contain no model calls. Item 7 and item 10 are doc-level scenarios.
6. Item 8's URL uses `/tree/` (a directory) instead of `/blob/` because the item is a package of five files.
7. Selected count (10) exceeds the brief's target of about 6.
8. Source text mentions model ids from several vendors (for example in agent constructors); they are not copied into items.
   Items record provider names only in `features.connectors`.

### Unresolved disagreements and remaining doubts

1. **Item 5, `supervisor-delegation`.** The triage agent can call `consult_specialist` and `consult_senior_doctor` any number of times and decides
   when to stop, and its docstring describes two delegation levels (L7-L13). However, the instructions (L156-L177) steer it towards one
   consultation or one escalation. Each tool also returns a ready `TriageFinalOutput` that the agent will usually pass on. Repeated delegation is
   therefore permitted, not designed. I kept the tag because the manager stays in control after each delegation, as other ledgers in this cluster
   define it. A stricter reading would leave `agent-tool-loop+agent-as-tool`. Cross-platform consistency is itself unsettled: the agno ledger tags
   `supervisor-delegation` instead of `agent-as-tool` for delegate tools, while crewai tags both.

   `pydantic_graph` example at this sha, since `question_graph` and persistence were removed in V2. If the merged agentic cluster requires a model

   are SCC nodes with an in-edge from outside") counts only top-level SCC entries, so it would report this item as single-entry.

## How verdicts were assigned (conventions the merge may want to revisit)

1. Same conventions as the sibling `autogen` ledger. `native` only when the item maps to a static DAG, `map`, a bounded `loop`, typed tool-free agent calls, `code` steps and `human` nodes at node boundaries. A tool call whose arguments the model fills is an agent step plus a `task`. Loops the source leaves uncapped are still counted native when a cap is the only change, and the cap is named in `ir.notes`.
2. `agent-tool-loop` is tagged whenever a model calls tools and sees results inside one step, including provider-hosted tool loops (web search through the Responses API, code interpreter in an assistant), because a Foundry `agent` step has no tools.
3. `llm-router` + `group-chat` together when a model picks the speaker over a shared transcript. Where the selector prompt only encodes an alternation (item 7) a loop could reproduce today's behaviour, and the note says so, but the extension is kept because the choice is made by a model.
4. `interrupt-resume` only for the pause inside a node (item 6, `input()` inside a tool call). The handoff human callback (item 2) and the scripted user steps (items 7, 8) pause between agent turns, so they are `human` nodes in a loop.
5. `subworkflow-call` for `AddStepFromProcess` children. They are statically known, so compile-time inlining is possible; the note says what that loses. In item 10 the fish and potato children are drawn expanded because they hold the cycles, and `features.subworkflows` is 4 (the root's children) while the graph has 2 `subworkflow` nodes.
6. `signal-wait` was not tagged for item 9: the approve/reject events arrive at a known point and map to one `human` node with a typed answer. `webhook-trigger` was tagged for the gRPC request that starts the process.
7. Summarisation and truncation reducers (item 7) are tagged `context-compaction`. Sibling AutoGen ledger treated fixed message windows as code slices; here the summarisation reducer is a model call that rewrites the history, so it is not a window.
8. Mock tools are marked by what the source does (mock calendar create: write; mock weather lookup: read; mock refund and return: write), and the notes say that real services would be external effects.

## Findings kept as raw observations (code reading, nothing run)

- Magentic: `max_round_count` and `max_reset_count` default to None and the sample sets neither (`magentic.py:L137-L141`, `step5_magentic.py:L82-L86`), so the run is unbounded as written. Replan resets the stall count but not `round_count` (`L117-L125`). A malformed ledger is parsed once and not retried (`L463`).
- Plan-and-execute: `ExecuteStep.current_index` survives a replan (`plan_and_execute.py:L171-L191`), so after a replan the index points into the new list and tasks can be skipped. The executor returns the index of the task it just ran (`L193-L197`), so the "index >= len(plan)" finish test (`L236-L244`) never fires after the last task; the judge is called once more, and the sample output shows exactly three "continue" decisions for a three-task plan (`L388-L390`).
- Document generator: the terminator checks the substring "no" before "yes" (`custom_termination_strategy.py:L65-L68`), so "yes, no issues" reads as not approved. The termination model runs after every assistant message including the user agent (`agent_group_chat.py:L156-L160`). An out-of-range selector index is not retried (`custom_selection_strategy.py:L68`).
- Group chat with a chat-completion manager: the first stop check runs before any persona has spoken, and with `max_rounds=10` at most ten persona turns run (`group_chat.py:L164-L179`).
- Concurrent orchestration: results are collected in arrival order (`concurrent.py:L121-L122`); `structured_outputs_transform` keeps one chat history for all invocations (`tools.py:L45`, `L55`).
- Handoff: no turn cap; the run ends only when an agent calls `complete_task`, or after one reply when no human function is set (`handoffs.py:L235-L249`, `L308-L312`).
- Step04 delegated group chat: the scripted user step emits `Exit`, not `UserInputComplete`, when its list runs out (`ScriptedUserInputStep.cs:L84-L88`), so the user-input to done edge is never taken in the sample. The `AgentGroupChat` is a singleton whose history is not reset between delegations (`AgentGroupChatStep.cs:L27-L29`, reset commented out).
- Account opening: `NewAccountStep` builds the account id with `new Guid()`, an all-zero id (`NewAccountStep.cs:L22`). Credit and fraud checks are mock rules on one birth date and one user id (`CreditScoreCheckStep.cs:L24`, `FraudDetectionStep.cs:L22`).
- Document generation process: the proofreading loop and the user-rejection loop have no cap; the false branch of the publish step only skips the console write but the step still returns the draft, so a publish event would still be emitted (`PublishDocumentationStep.cs:L19-L28`); the service only ever sends `true` (`DocumentGenerationService.cs:L125-L131`).
- Food order: the dispatch `switch` has a default that emits nothing, so an unknown dish ends the run silently (`SingleFoodItemProcess.cs:L99-L115`); frying fails at random about half the time with no retry cap (`FryFoodStep.cs:L33-L36`).

- `validate-sk.mjs` (imports `validateItem`, `parseVerdict`, `findSecret`, `NON_REDISTRIBUTABLE_LICENCE`, `CATEGORIES`, `CONSTRUCT_IDS`, `graphFeatures` from `research/corpus-20261006/scripts/check-items.mjs`) reports 0 problems over 10 lines: every line parses as JSON; unique ids; every required field present; every category and effect in the vocabulary; every edge endpoint is a node id; no isolated node; every non-trigger node has an inbound edge and every node is reachable from a trigger; descriptions at most 400 characters (maximum 326); node summaries at most 200 characters; `parseVerdict` parses all 10 verdicts; verdict tokens are in registry order (existing ids first, candidate ids in the order given in the task) and each token appears in `ir.notes` and every via-extension note cites `path:Lx-Ly` spans; `findSecret` finds nothing in any full line; `rawPath`, `url` and `revision` agree with the id and the pinned sha; every `extraction.spans` entry points at an existing file and a line range inside it (lines counted at the pinned revision); the licence policy gives `redistributable: true` for MIT; node, edge, fan-out, effect, human-step, code and model-call features equal the graph-derived values; human-step items declare `wait` in `async`; `webhook-trigger` has `webhook` in `async`.
- Control: a deliberately corrupted copy (dangling edge, 201-character summary, wrong token order, out-of-range span, secret-shaped title, GPL licence with `redistributable: true`, orphan node, unknown construct) produced 17 problem lines, so the validator does fail on each defect class.
- `node scripts/check-items.mjs semantic-kernel.jsonl` prints, verbatim (first lines): `10 lines, 0 valid, 10 invalid` / `source.extra-key: 10` / `unexpected source.extraction` (exit 1). Cause: `SOURCE_KEYS` in `scripts/check-items.mjs` lacks `extraction`, while the task schema requires `source.extraction = {method, spans, extractor}`. ### Rules applied

These follow the verified sibling parts so that the merge sees one convention.

1. **`agent-tool-loop`.** Assigned when a model is offered tools it may choose among and the results return to a model. This includes provider-hosted tools such as code interpreter and Responses web search. A model whose search happens inside the model service, with no tool schema passed (Magentic `gpt-4o-search-preview`), is an external-effect model call and does not by itself qualify.
2. **`llm-router`.** Assigned when a separate model call (selector, manager or ledger) picks the next agent among declared targets and is re-entered in a cycle. It is not assigned in two cases:
   - a working agent hands itself off (`handoff`);
   - a one-shot typed verdict inside a loop, such as plan-and-execute's continue-or-replan or Step04's intent classifier. That maps to an enum `agent` plus `when` guards, so it is native.
3. **`group-chat`.** Assigned when participants receive one broadcast transcript and a speaker is selected among them.
4. **`context-compaction`.** Reserved for in-place summarisation or trimming of a working conversation. A model call whose summary output becomes the next step's explicit input is an ordinary typed `agent` node. A fixed last-N window is a `code` slice.
5. **Agentic scope.** An item without any model or agent step is dropped from this cluster, even when it has loops or routers. Deterministic workflows belong to the orchestration cluster.

### Disagreements and doubts not resolved

1. **`context-compaction` boundary (item 7).** The extractor's convention 7 treats any summarisation reducer as compaction. This pass treats a summary that becomes an explicit step input as a native `agent` call (rule 4). If the merge adopts the extractor's reading, item 7 regains `context-compaction`. No other item is affected.
2. **`llm-router` for handoff with several targets (item 2).** AG2's verification tags it when two or more transfer functions are offered at once; AutoGen's does not. The triage agent offers three targets. The tag is left off and the doubt is recorded in the notes.
3. **Speaker selection that only alternates (item 7).** The selector prompt fixes a strict calendar/weather alternation and sees only the last message. `llm-router+group-chat` follows the convention that a model makes the choice. A behavioural reading would make it a native two-agent loop.
4. **`subworkflow-call` for statically built child processes (item 8).** `AddStepFromProcess` children are built in code at definition time. COVERAGE.md §1 counts compile-time-inlined children (KFP, ComfyUI) as native. The agentic parts (burr, langgraph) keep `subworkflow-call` for subgraphs, so it was kept here.
5. **Human node versus `signal-wait` (item 9).** The approve and reject events are process input events posted to the instance by id over gRPC. They are not ordered after the review request. The `human` reading assumes the intended order, and a strict reading of the event semantics would add `signal-wait`.
6. **Uncapped loops counted as needing only a cap.** These are item 1 (Magentic caps unset), item 2 (no turn cap), item 5 (no iteration cap) and item 9 (both revision loops). The verdicts do not mark "a cap had to be added". This doubt is the same one recorded in the AutoGen verification.
7. **Library internals not read.** No claim depends on them, but three things were not read: ChatCompletionAgent's default function-choice behaviour (item 2's auto-invocation is confirmed by the sample output instead), the .NET `AgentGroupChat` and `ChatHistorySummarizationReducer` sources (item 7), and the Process runtime's parameter-retention semantics (item 9's publish join).
8. **Effect labels for mocks.** Item 8's `mail` is `external` while it only prints. Item 7's render nodes are `write` for console output. Both were left as the extractor labelled them: the semantic labelling convention, extractor convention 8.

## 5. Modelling conventions (read before comparing with other clusters)

- **Node granularity.** One node per agent. When `planning_interval` is set, the periodic planning model call is its own node (items 1 and 3) because it is a separate model call with its own prompt. A CodeAgent acts by writing code, so tool calls are made from inside the executor: the graph has `agent -> python_executor -> tool` and `tool -> python_executor` return edges. A ToolCallingAgent calls tools directly. A managed agent is a model node entered from the executor and returning to it. Tools that wrap a single model call (`visualizer`, `inspect_file_as_text`) are `model` nodes; tools that fetch, search or drive a browser are `action` nodes. Step callbacks that edit memory are nodes (items 3 and 4).
- **Loop edges.** ReAct returns, tool-result returns, periodic re-planning and the resume path are `loop` edges, so removing them leaves a DAG (checked for all 7 items; every node is reachable from a root).
- **Effects.** smolagents tools declare none. They were assigned from the tool code: HTTP or Hub calls are `external`, local file or index reads are `read`, local file writes and printing are `write`. The executor is `external` when the import allowlist is lifted or the browser library is allowed (items 1 and 4) and `none` with the default allowlist.
- **`features.branching`** counts decision points in the source flow where a model, a person or code picks one of several successors (final answer or another step, approve/modify/cancel, extension dispatch, try/except, config switches). **`features.loops`** counts iteration constructs on the control path (agent ReAct loops, thread-pool maps, per-file loops, the resume re-entry). Console re-prompt loops inside a human node are not counted. The merge recomputes graph-derived fields anyway; `hasCode` is false for item 2 only because its team is one `subworkflow` node.
- **Verdict basis.** Every smolagents agent is a model-in-a-loop with a run-time number of steps, so `agent-tool-loop` is in all 7 verdicts, and every CodeAgent adds `model-generated-code-exec` because the action language is Python written by the model at run time (the Foundry `code` node is authored ahead of time). That is why no item is native. Native sub-parts are named in each item's notes (map over runtime lists, extension dispatch, single typed model calls, JSONL appends, an indexing pipeline).
- **Where a catch-and-record is not `error-branch`.** Items 2 and 7 catch any exception around an agent run, store the failure in the result row and continue. `onError: continue` on the node plus a `when` guard on the failure output covers that, so `error-branch` is not claimed (no sibling agentic item claims it either). If a reviewer holds that the IR's `onError` does not reach an executor node, add `error-branch` to items 2 and 7.
- **Subworkflow.** Item 2 draws the team as one `subworkflow` node because `create_agent_team` is fixed code called once per question. `subworkflow-call` is not claimed: the callee is a statically known definition (inlinable), and the dynamic part (how often and with which task strings the manager calls the search agent) is `supervisor-delegation` and `agent-as-tool`.
- **Token order inside a verdict.** Existing registry ids in registry order, then the task-list ids in task-list order, then `new-*` ids.

### Construct use

Counts over the 7 items: agent-tool-loop 7, model-generated-code-exec 7, multimodal-io 3, supervisor-delegation 2, agent-as-tool 2, interrupt-resume 1, context-compaction 1, partial-output-stream 1, guardrail-tripwire 1, new-live-session-handle 1. Existing registry ids used: agent-tool-loop only. Candidate new agentic ids used (exact spellings): `supervisor-delegation`, `interrupt-resume`, `agent-as-tool`, `guardrail-tripwire`, `partial-output-stream`, `model-generated-code-exec`, `multimodal-io`, `context-compaction`.

One `new-*` id was used, and it is not new to the cluster: **`new-live-session-handle`** (item 4). The langgraph extractor defined it for `langgraph:langgraph/docs/docs/tutorials/web-navigation/web_voyager.ipynb`, and the same definition was reused here: a long-lived external session object (a browser page or driver, a database connection, a sandbox) that is created before the run, held in a variable that many nodes read and mutate, and cannot be serialised into the run record, so it cannot be journaled, suspended or replayed from JSON state; the IR would need a named session capability with open/close and replay semantics. In item 4 it is the Chrome driver started by `helium.start_chrome` (`web_browser.md:L88`), read by the three tools (L54, L66, L74) and the screenshot callback (L93) and mutated by the model's code.

Considered and not used, with reason:

| construct | why not |
| --- | --- |
| handoff | In every hierarchy the manager keeps control; the managed agent returns a report (`agents.py:L868-L890`). The sub-agent's clarification request (`run.py:L97-L99`) comes back as a result, not as a transfer. |
| llm-router | The manager and the agents choose among tools by writing code or JSON tool calls: that is the tool loop, not routing among declared nodes. Item 7's switch is a command-line input, not a model choice. |
| group-chat, dynamic-agent-spawn | No shared conversation among peers; every agent is constructed from fixed code before the run. |
| state-reducer | Nothing merges parallel writes into one key. ToolCallingAgent runs parallel tool calls but concatenates their observations in id order (`agents.py:L1436-L1442`). |
| shared-scratchpad | Each agent has its own `state` dict (`agents.py:L331`); `additional_args` are copied into the callee's state per call (`agents.py:L471-L475`), a one-way parameter pass, not a board. |
| checkpoint-rewind | Memory can be edited and continued in process (items 3 and 6), but no checkpoint is persisted or forked. |
| cross-run-state, chat-session | `agent.run` resets memory by default (`agents.py:L478-L480`). Resumable batches (items 2 and 7) read the previous results file as an input. See the observation on executor state in section 8. |
| guardrail-tripwire (items 1-5, 7) | Only item 6 has validators. Item 2's `final_answer_checks` hook is token accounting and always returns true by intent. |
| interrupt-resume (items 1, 2, 4-7) | No person is consulted inside those loops. The library also ships a `UserInputTool` (`default_tools.py:L93-L101`) that would ask a person from inside a tool call; no selected example uses it. |
| partial-output-stream (items 1-4, 6, 7) | `stream_outputs` is left at its default False. |
| context-compaction (items 1-3, 5-7) | Summary mode drops the system prompt and earlier plans for the planning call (`agents.py:L684`, `memory.py:L174-L176`) and omits model outputs in a managed agent's summary of work (`memory.py:L94`); that is not a reduction to fit a context window. Item 4 is the only explicit trimming. |
